title: Running a Namespace: The Controls and Economics of RWA ID for Platforms

The registry is on Robinhood Chain; names resolve on Ethereum mainnet through ENS. Our first article explained why tokenized-asset platforms need a readable, platform-controlled identity layer. This one is for the people who would run it: product owners deciding on onboarding flows, finance teams modelling cost and revenue, and engineers who need to know exactly which wallet signs what. The architecture in one line: the registry, which holds your namespace, allowlists, names, fees and sponsor pool, lives on Robinhood Chain (chain id 4663), and your clients’ names resolve on Ethereum mainnet through ENS . Everything below happens on the Robinhood Chain side. Resolution in wallets takes care of itself. The console Platforms manage a namespace at rwa-id.com/console , also served at dashboard.rwa-id.com. The console is a static application that reads Robinhood Chain directly from your browser. There’s no RWA ID backend, indexer or account to create. You connect the wallet that owns the namespace, and every change is a transaction that wallet signs, costing a fraction of a cent in gas. The console is organised around the tasks a platform performs: Overview : claims, revocations and usage for the namespace. Allowlist : upload and publish who can claim. Claim fee and Treasury : what a claim costs and where your share goes. Sponsorship : fund or drain the sponsor pool, and deliver names with claimFor . Transferability : soulbound or transferable, per namespace or per name. Artwork : the image every name in your namespace shows. Availability : pause and resume claiming. Registry : look up any name and revoke it. Ownership : hand the namespace to another wallet or Safe. Creating a namespace is free. You choose a permanent slug, a treasury address, a claim fee and the default transferability, and the connecting wallet becomes the project owner. The allowlist workflow The allowlist is a CSV of name,wallet pairs. When you upload it, the console builds a Merkle tree in your browser, pins the proof set to IPFS and asks your wallet to publish a single 32-byte root on-chain. Your client list never passes through an RWA ID server. In practice: Adding clients. Load the live proof set, append the new rows and republish. Names already claimed are unaffected by a new root. Stale links fail cleanly. The claim page checks that its proof set matches the live root, so a client with an outdated link sees an explanation instead of a failed transaction. Privacy. The pinned proof set is public and permanent: it lists every label and wallet. Use pseudonymous labels rather than legal names unless you have a lawful basis to publish them. The link between a name and a verified client belongs in your own records. Naming rules. Labels follow ENS normalisation rules, using lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Anything a wallet would rewrite is rejected at claim time, so every name that mints also resolves. Fees, treasury and the 70/30 split Every claim pays a fee in USDG on Robinhood Chain. You set the fee, subject to a protocol floor of 0.50 USDG. The fee is split in the claim transaction itself and paid straight out: 70% to your treasury and 30% to the protocol. The registry never holds fees in escrow. Your feeClient paysYour treasuryProtocolBelow 0.500.50 USDG0.350.151.00 USDG1.000.700.305.00 USDG5.003.501.50 You can change the fee and the treasury address at any time from the console. effectiveClaimFee returns the current price of a claim, and projectUsage reports total claims and protocol fees for your namespace. Finance teams can reconcile directly against the chain. Sponsored onboarding: sponsor pools and claimFor Many institutional platforms won’t want clients approving a stablecoin payment just to receive a name. Two features remove that step. Sponsor pools. Any wallet can fund your namespace’s pool in USDG, and only the project owner can withdraw from it. When the pool holds at least one full fee, the pool pays and the client pays nothing. A partly funded pool is left alone rather than split between two payers. The protocol’s recovery function is walled off from sponsor balances, so it can’t touch them. Because the 70/30 split still runs on sponsored claims, your 70% flows back to your own treasury. At the floor, a sponsored claim costs the platform 0.15 USDG. Onboarding 10,000 clients at the floor means funding 5,000 USDG, of which 3,500 returns to your treasury, for a net cost of 1,500 USDG plus gas. claimFor. Each allowlist entry binds a name to one wallet, so anyone can submit a claim on a client’s behalf and the name still mints only to that client’s wallet. From the console’s Sponsorship screen, a platform can deliver names to its allowlist directly. Clients don’t visit a page, hold gas or sign anything. If the pool doesn’t cover a fee, claimFor charges the sending wallet instead, so keep the pool funded before bulk delivery. Name policy Soulbound or transferable. Set a default for the namespace and override it per name. Soulbound is the usual choice for client identities. Transferable names resolve to their new holder automatically. Artwork.
